motion: Does divine hiddenness provide good evidence against God's existence?

moves.sectionTitle: Hiddenness, cultural contingency, and religious diversity
moves.currentDescription: Baggini infers that God's nonexistence more simply predicts the absence of clear divine evidence than does a personal deity whose recognition might matter.
moves.lockedProposition: The simplest explanation for the absence of clear evidence of God is that God does not exist.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: know there's no clear way of of knowing that it's there right so people who believe in God believe in something which is in some ways hidden from us and that's a problem because if you there are plenty people who don't believe in God or gods and they would say the most simple explanation for why we can't clearly see evidence for the existence of this being is that it's not there you
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: The move immediately converts hiddenness into a comparative explanation, reasoning that nonexistent agents predict absent public evidence more straightforwardly than a recognition-seeking personal deity, which gives it excellent motion relevance and substantial responsiveness. Principal limitation: The excerpt supplies no developed likelihood comparison, specification of expected revelation, or evidence showing why possible divine purposes cannot offset the proposed simplicity, leaving evidential warrant markedly below its relevance. Live burden: Baggini still must identify the relevant conception of God, explain what clarity that being would probably provide, and answer ambiguity-based reasons rather than relying principally on intuitive obviousness.

moves.sectionTitle: Hiddenness, cultural contingency, and religious diversity
moves.currentDescription: Baker-Hytch argues that mixed evidence can rationally favor one conclusion while still leaving conscientious disagreement reasonable, without implying that every worldview is equally supported.
moves.lockedProposition: Evidential ambiguity permits a reasonable conclusion while also permitting conscientious, rational disagreement because different evidence points in different directions.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: because I think um you can come to a reasonable conclusion and and as I said I think that the evidence does tip a certain way does point in a certain direction but there's a sense in which um reasonable people can disagree about it and um there's a sense in which um if you take all of the different bits of evidence if you isolated some of them they would point in a very different direction to the way in which some other bits of the evidence would point and that's not saying oh it's just a freefor all um you know the evidence is completely indecisive it's not saying that so I basically have wanted to say
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baker-Hytch carefully distinguishes directional evidence from decisive evidence, allowing a rational conclusion alongside reasonable disagreement and thereby establishing a coherent, charitable framework for interpreting the debate's conflicting considerations. Principal limitation: The framework remains largely programmatic because this move neither inventories the evidence nor demonstrates which considerations favor theism, so its evidential warrant depends on later cumulative development. Live burden: He must show that ambiguity is expected enough under traditional theism, answer the cultural-diversity challenge, and establish that positive evidence genuinely counterbalances hiddenness rather than merely permitting abstract disagreement.

moves.sectionTitle: Hiddenness, cultural contingency, and religious diversity
moves.currentDescription: Baggini links belief's dependence on birthplace, era, history, and character to the inference that a hidden God would not make correct recognition crucial.
moves.lockedProposition: Because belief is largely determined by history, location, era, and character outside one's control, a hidden God is unlikely to make correct belief crucial.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: so if there were a God how could it be important to that God how could it matter to them what I happen to believe because what I happen to believe is going to be largely dictated by my my history my my place on Earth my time of Earth my character Etc if if it's and so that that is all things that are kind of out of my control so so it seemed really weird I was I was growing up struggling with my faith thinking it surely it really matters whether I believe in God God or not and I thought well a god who's just so mysterious if that God exists probably cares much less about whether we believe in it or not than a lot of religious leaders would would would have you
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baggini connects familiar determinants of religious belief, including location, historical period, personal history, and character, to a pointed fairness inference about whether a hidden God could reasonably make correct recognition crucial. Principal limitation: The move asserts that these factors largely dictate belief without supplying comparative evidence, and it moves from reduced control to divine indifference without excluding nonpunitive or noncreedal forms of personal theism. Live burden: He must establish the strength of cultural determination, distinguish epistemic access from salvific consequences, and show why a loving God could not value relationship while judging honest error permissively.

moves.sectionTitle: Hiddenness, cultural contingency, and religious diversity
moves.currentDescription: Baggini grants that general arguments may suggest mysterious ultimacy, but cultural emergence and contradiction among religions block the inference to any specific revelation.
moves.lockedProposition: Arguments about ultimacy may support agnosticism or a mysterious source, but religious diversity and cultural emergence block the further inference to any specific traditional religion.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baggini grants the intellectually respectable possibility of mysterious ultimacy, then sharply separates that modest conclusion from specific religion by invoking culturally generated, mutually incompatible traditions as stronger counterevidence to revelation. Principal limitation: Calling religions human inventions and treating diversity as overwhelming evidence outpaces the supplied support, since disagreement alone does not determine whether one tradition retains independent historical or philosophical warrant. Live burden: He must compare human-construction and revelation hypotheses more explicitly, engage Baker-Hytch's prospective cumulative evidence, and explain why generic theism cannot legitimately alter historical likelihoods.

moves.sectionTitle: Probabilistic hiddenness, coercion, and relational goods
moves.currentDescription: Baggini agrees that arguments for God, evil, and hiddenness operate probabilistically rather than deductively, constraining both sides to evidential claims below proof.
moves.lockedProposition: The debate should be probabilistic: neither arguments for God nor the problems of evil and hiddenness amount to deductive proof.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: so I think where we would agree I think is this idea that we're not looking for like logical incompatibility or logical proof I think one of the problems I have traditionally perhaps sometimes the way philosophy of religion was taught particularly at school level was we had these like arguments through the existence of God as though they were meant to be you know knocked down proofs you know sometimes they called them proofs they're not proofs none of them are proofs I think that even even you think they're strong arguments and I don't you know they they fall far shot of proof in a similar way the problem of evil is a problem it's not a disproof of God right so I think that's the first
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baggini directly accepts Baker-Hytch's distinction between evidence and proof, symmetrically applying it to theistic arguments, evil, and hiddenness while clearly calibrating his own burden as probabilistic rather than deductive. Principal limitation: Agreement about argumentative form does little by itself to establish how strongly hiddenness favors atheism, and the move offers no likelihood comparison or substantive evidence beyond methodological clarification. Live burden: He must now quantify at least comparatively what hiddenness predicts under rival hypotheses and demonstrate that his cultural and relational considerations outweigh the positive evidence Baker-Hytch promises.

moves.sectionTitle: Probabilistic hiddenness, coercion, and relational goods
moves.currentDescription: Baker-Hytch argues possible divine reasons defeat deductive incompatibility while conceding hiddenness as powerful probabilistic counterevidence requiring assessment beside the positive theistic case.
moves.lockedProposition: Possible divine reasons defeat a deductive incompatibility claim, although hiddenness remains powerful probabilistic evidence against traditional theism that must be weighed against evidence on the other side.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baker-Hytch precisely separates logical compatibility from probabilistic support, explains how merely possible divine reasons answer the former, and candidly concedes hiddenness and evil as powerful evidence against traditional theism. Principal limitation: Possibility defeats entailment but does not establish probability, and this move has not yet warranted any particular divine reason or supplied the countervailing evidence needed for the promised cumulative comparison. Live burden: He must show that relational goods make some ambiguity more than speculative, specify the positive philosophical and historical case, and explain its comparative weight against acknowledged hiddenness.

moves.sectionTitle: Probabilistic hiddenness, coercion, and relational goods
moves.currentDescription: Baggini replies that, conditional on God's existence, continued hiddenness more naturally suggests divine indifference toward correct recognition and worship than a delicate relational strategy.
moves.lockedProposition: If God exists yet remains hidden, the simplest explanation is that God does not greatly care whether humans correctly recognize or worship God.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: hidden again you know if we go for the most obvious explanation the most obvious explanation would be the reason why God would keep himself hidden from us is that it's not important for him that we recognize who he is and and worship Him Etc right um that seems to be the most simplest explanation so it goes back to one can believe in a god that is hidden and think well you know we who knows the mind of God anyway who knows what's God reasons but the very fact that God is hidden seems to be very good reason to think that if a God exists it's not really half as bothered about whether we pray to the right one or not as as our religious leaders have made us think so I think that is a really strong and obvious clear bit of
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baggini responds directly to the coercion proposal with a clear competing explanation, inferring that a hidden deity probably cares less about exact recognition or worship than religious authorities commonly suggest. Principal limitation: Describing indifference as simplest does not compare its probability with noncoercive relationship, soul-making, or permissive judgment, and the supporting evidence remains the same observed hiddenness whose interpretation is disputed. Live burden: He must show why reduced concern predicts the world's particular ambiguity better than relational restraint and distinguish indifference to creedal accuracy from indifference to freely formed relationship.

moves.sectionTitle: Probabilistic hiddenness, coercion, and relational goods
moves.currentDescription: Baker-Hytch proposes that overwhelming divine visibility could distort motivation or coerce response, so reduced obviousness may protect freer relationship despite remaining counterevidence.
moves.lockedProposition: A personal God may permit ambiguity because overwhelming manifestation would distort or coerce human response, while hiddenness still counts as evidence against God.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baker-Hytch supplies a concrete relational good that could make some ambiguity intelligible, using the disguised-monarch parable to explain how overwhelming power might distort motivation while retaining his concession that hiddenness counts against God. Principal limitation: The analogy concerns concealment of royal status rather than existence, and the psychological claim that clearer divine awareness would coerce love is asserted without evidence or comparison to less hidden alternatives. Live burden: He must explain why an omnipotent God could not disclose existence without overwhelming agency, why ambiguity is distributed geographically, and how the proposed benefit outweighs nonresistant nonbelief.

moves.sectionTitle: Probabilistic hiddenness, coercion, and relational goods
moves.currentDescription: Baggini answers that the disguised king reveals his existence, while geographically contingent religious recognition makes ambiguity badly fitted to securing freely chosen divine relationship.
moves.lockedProposition: The king analogy conceals status rather than existence, and the geographic contingency of belief makes hiddenness a poor mechanism for securing free relationship.

Principal limitation: The geographic premise is presented impressionistically, and the rebuttal does not exclude broad awareness of divinity or explain why relationship must begin with doctrinally specific recognition rather than partial disclosure. Live burden: He must substantiate geographic dominance, address Baker-Hytch's high-god distinction, and connect uneven affiliation to God's existence rather than only to particular punitive or exclusivist theologies.

moves.sectionTitle: Probabilistic hiddenness, coercion, and relational goods
moves.currentDescription: Baker-Hytch invokes widespread high-god awareness to preserve the disguised-king analogy, yet concedes that eternal consequences tied to geographically accidental doctrines are indefensible.

Principal limitation: The claimed prevalence of high-god belief is referenced rather than demonstrated, its content may not amount to awareness of one personal God, and the move does not answer nonbelievers who lack even generic recognition. Live burden: He must establish the empirical generalization, explain exceptions and cultural variation, and show that generic awareness plus hidden status actually protects freedom better than clearer disclosure.

moves.sectionTitle: Personal experience and sincere seeking
moves.currentDescription: Baggini argues personal encounter usually grounds Christian faith, whereas philosophical apologetics often repairs tensions between antecedent commitment and problems such as evil or hiddenness.
moves.lockedProposition: Personal religious experience usually grounds Christian belief, while philosophical apologetics often preserves an antecedent faith against problems such as evil and hiddenness.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baggini offers a recognizable epistemic sequence in which powerful personal experience grounds faith and apologetic reasoning subsequently reconciles that commitment with evil or hiddenness, clarifying what he thinks actually motivates belief. Live burden: He must substantiate the prevalence and causal priority of experience, distinguish genealogy from justification, and connect culturally mediated experiences to the probability of God's nonexistence.

moves.sectionTitle: Personal experience and sincere seeking
moves.currentDescription: Baker-Hytch explicitly agrees that perceived personal encounter with God grounds most people's faith, confirming the shared experiential premise without endorsing Baggini's debunking inference.
moves.lockedProposition: Personal encounter with God does ground most people's faith.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baker-Hytch gives an exact, unambiguous answer to Baggini's empirical question, creating direct response contact and narrowing disagreement by accepting that personal encounter commonly grounds faith. Principal limitation: The bare concession contains no evidence for the prevalence claim, says nothing about experience's reliability, and neither accepts nor answers the further contention that apologetics rationalizes antecedent commitment. Live burden: He must distinguish experiential grounding from objective justification, address cultural shaping and diversity, and explain how experience contributes within his cumulative case without carrying discriminatory weight it cannot bear.

moves.sectionTitle: Personal experience and sincere seeking
moves.currentDescription: Baker-Hytch argues unanswered seekers' openness is difficult to diagnose, using his formerly instrumental prayers cautiously while refusing to generalize that psychology to every nonbeliever.
moves.lockedProposition: Cases of apparently sincere but unanswered seeking are psychologically underdetermined, and Baker-Hytch's own earlier instrumental prayers cannot be generalized to every nonbeliever.

moves.sectionTitle: Historical evidence, psychology, and rational inquiry

moves.lockedProposition: Jesus's historical existence and basic career are academically secure, although further argument is needed to infer that he was God incarnate.

moves.sectionTitle: Historical evidence, psychology, and rational inquiry
moves.currentDescription: Baggini credits religion's humility, community, care, and reverence while arguing those goods neither require nor justify making precise creedal assent a moral litmus test.
moves.lockedProposition: Religion has valuable ethical and communal functions, but it goes wrong when precise belief becomes the litmus test of moral or religious worth.

Live burden: He must explain whether religious goods bear on God's existence, show how cultural contingency undermines creedal requirements, and respond directly to the claim that psychological origins never settle truth.

moves.lockedProposition: Religion may provide psychological comfort, but causal explanations of belief do not settle truth and analogous motivational explanations can be applied to unbelief.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baker-Hytch cleanly separates a belief's causal psychology from its evidential merits and applies motivational scrutiny symmetrically, conceding religious comfort while noting that unbelief may also involve preferences. Principal limitation: The reverse-direction example concerns an individual's reported motivation and does not establish general symmetry, while the distinction alone cannot rescue evidence whose formation is systematically culture-sensitive or unreliable. Live burden: He must evaluate whether the proposed genealogy actually tracks epistemic unreliability, connect independent reasons to theism, and avoid treating possible atheist motivation as an answer to religious evidence.

moves.sectionTitle: Historical evidence, psychology, and rational inquiry
moves.currentDescription: Baggini argues reasoning depends on prior worldview networks, so epistemic integrity requires humility, motivational honesty, and close attention to facts beyond internal coherence.
moves.lockedProposition: Rationality operates within networks of prior belief, so honest attention to motives and facts, rather than clever coherence alone, is necessary because any thinker may occupy a distorted worldview.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baggini develops a balanced epistemic standard, explaining how intelligent reasoning can remain internally coherent within distorted belief networks and therefore require humility, motivational honesty, and close attention to public facts. Principal limitation: The historical analogy illustrates worldview dependence but supplies no procedure for deciding between theism and atheism, and the move's connection to hiddenness remains indirect. Live burden: He must operationalize integrity beyond personal sincerity, identify which shared facts discriminate between rival worldviews, and demonstrate that religious commitments are more distortion-prone than his own starting assumptions.

moves.sectionTitle: Historical evidence, psychology, and rational inquiry
moves.currentDescription: Baker-Hytch accepts worldview humility but adds that skepticism becomes unreliable when selectively aimed at disfavored authorities while favored beliefs escape equivalent scrutiny.
moves.lockedProposition: Healthy skepticism must be applied consistently; selective skepticism preserves favored beliefs without subjecting them to equivalent scrutiny.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: I mean I pretty much agree with everything Julian just said there um I think um one thing that um I often feel about people who let's say don't believe that the Earth is round is that in a way that they've applied skepticism which is just you know the to to be skeptical about something is to um is to doubt it in some way to call into question question uh the evidence supporting something which is a perfectly healthy thing to do but I think what often goes wrong with the sort of conspiracy theory type beliefs like Flat Earth for example is that the the skepticism has been applied in a very selective way so that um you're skeptical about the about the things that NASA say or about certain um scientific bodies and so on but um actually if you were to apply the same kind of skepticism across the board um you should believe a lot less things than you actually do so it's a bit of a kind of targeted skepticism and I think actually so you know philosophers like to think about radical skepticism so I've just been teaching uh deart this term and so dayart engaged in this sort of thought experiment of like let's kind of doubt everything that I can possibly doubt and kind of try and bracket out and and sort of um at least pretend that I don't believe any of the things I normally do and then let's let's kind of see what's left and it's an interesting thought experiment to do but but so yeah as I said I think the problem is these people who engage in um conspiracy theory type thinking often they they actually if if anything haven't gone far enough with their skepticism because I think then they'd see there's actually way more stuff they should disbelieve if they were going to be consistent
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baker-Hytch accepts Baggini's humility principle and adds a clear consistency requirement, using selective distrust in conspiracy thinking to illustrate why skepticism must scrutinize accepted and rejected claims symmetrically. Principal limitation: The example does not show that Baggini applies skepticism selectively, and the move never identifies a specific theistic consideration receiving unequal treatment, weakening both response contact and motion relevance. Live burden: He must demonstrate an actual asymmetry in the debate, apply equivalent standards to religious testimony and institutions, and explain how consistent skepticism improves the cumulative case for God.

moves.sectionTitle: Pluralism, experiential diversity, judgment, and the cumulative case
moves.currentDescription: Baggini defends humble, nonliteral, practice-centered pluralism as intellectually coherent and desirable while acknowledging that this model differs from most believers’ privileged doctrinal commitments.
moves.lockedProposition: A humble, nonliteral, practice-centered pluralism is coherent, but it differs from the privileged truth claims held by most religious believers.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: think that what you said is is is a very much a possibility but it requires a way of thinking about religion which for some people is isn't so far from what they have at the moment there are plenty of people who would say look okay I'm what I'm I'm a Jew I'm a Christian I'm a Hindu whatever it might be and you know what I don't really you know we don't really know what God is like but we're we're we're we're relating to God as best we can through our ways these we have our myths we have our stories it's imperfect this is the best we can do and other people who do other religions they're doing the same thing so we don't take our beliefs too literally we don't hold them too tightly we're just finding our ways to try and have contact with the Divine as best we can telling the kind of stories that work for us and in every religion you get people who are like that there are Christians like that who who think that the most important thing about Christianity is the practice rather than the doctrines and that they they're agnostic about whether you know the word god describes an entity or or something else and if if it were the case case that more religious people had that idea of their own religion I think that would be good I think it' be intellectually coherent I think it'd be fine I think you're saying the person who says they see the whole elephant is claiming a privileged position they are in a way but I think the way the metaphor goes over is they're saying that you know actually to be consistent about it you'd say you know actually even when I describe it as an elephant I'm just giving a perspective you know the ultimate perspective it wouldn't be even be an elephant who knows what it is from the ultimate perspective it's just a way of giving you the way in so it would be great but I I think unfortunately it really doesn't describe the way most people think about their own religion I think you know
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baggini directly absorbs the privileged-narrator objection by treating even the elephant description as perspectival, then articulates a coherent religious posture centered on modest stories, practice, and contact with divinity. Principal limitation: He concedes that this model does not describe most believers, and its attractiveness or coherence does not itself establish truth, explain hiddenness, or supply evidence against God's existence. Live burden: He must connect pluralism to the motion, justify the empirical claim about typical exclusivism, and show why multiple perspectives favor human construction over limited but genuine revelation.

moves.sectionTitle: Pluralism, experiential diversity, judgment, and the cumulative case
moves.currentDescription: Baker-Hytch argues that religious pluralism remains truth-exclusive because the elephant story’s narrator claims privileged knowledge of how limited religious perspectives relate to ultimate reality.
moves.lockedProposition: Religious pluralism deserves consideration but is itself truth-exclusive because its narrator claims a privileged view of how all traditions relate to reality.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baker-Hytch identifies the elephant analogy's hidden standpoint, reasoning that its narrator claims privileged knowledge of the whole and showing that pluralism cannot present itself as uniquely free from truth-excluding commitments. Principal limitation: Establishing that pluralism makes a substantive truth claim does not disprove it, answer religious diversity, or show that Christianity possesses stronger access to ultimate reality. Live burden: He must compare the evidence for pluralism and Christianity, explain how partial truths within other religions fit specific revelation, and reconnect this conceptual correction to hiddenness's evidential force.

moves.sectionTitle: Pluralism, experiential diversity, judgment, and the cumulative case
moves.currentDescription: Baggini argues culturally familiar content reveals prior beliefs shaping religious experience, so intense subjective conviction cannot transform those experiences into strong objective evidence.
moves.lockedProposition: Because prior expectations shape the content and interpretation of religious and near-death experiences, their subjective power does not make them good objective evidence.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: problem of well briefly yeah I mean I I I see it as a problem for the reasons I think the question are I mean how people people have religious experiences but how they receive it is almost invariably to do with you know their expectations and what their prior beliefs are and people do not spontaneously have visions of the Virgin Mary if they've never even heard who the Virgin Mary is right she only ever appears to people who've already had a very strong connection with them in certain ways so I think generally speaking that makes me think that you really should not trust this kind of experience as good evidence for anything the problem is that if you've had one of these experiences it can feel so powerful to you it's very hard for you to dismiss it like that so I think it's just an inherent problem here that there are certain things that if you take an objective look at them they just seem to be very obviously seem to be bad evidence but if you happen to have that experience yourself it's very very difficult to do that not impossible
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baggini connects culturally familiar visionary content to prior expectations and clearly distinguishes an experience's immense subjective force from its weaker capacity to provide publicly discriminating evidence between religions. Principal limitation: The Virgin Mary illustration is anecdotal and the near-universal shaping claim is unsupported, while cultural mediation does not by itself entail fabrication or eliminate every evidential contribution. Live burden: He must establish the prevalence and reliability implications of mediation, address reported cross-cultural experiences, and show why cumulative corroboration cannot rescue a modest role for experience.

moves.sectionTitle: Pluralism, experiential diversity, judgment, and the cumulative case
moves.currentDescription: Baker-Hytch rejects punishment for honest religious error outside human control, arguing such condemnation conflicts with perfect love and need not follow from biblical texts.
moves.lockedProposition: A perfectly loving God would not send people to hell for honest religious error caused by information outside their control.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: experiences yeah so certainly I don't uh go with the idea of a a loving God who is going to send people to hell because they got the wrong information and that was you know something that was not under their control that just seems very hard to square with the idea of a perfectly loving being and in fact and I you this would be a much longer conversation but I I actually don't think that that the biblical text um point in that direction Direction either
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baker-Hytch squarely accepts the fairness force of cultural contingency and limits its theological consequence, reasoning that perfect love is incompatible with condemning people for honest errors produced by information outside their control. Principal limitation: The claim relies mainly on moral-theological intuition, the biblical support is merely asserted, and removing punishment does not explain why a relationship-seeking God permits persistent mistaken recognition. Live burden: He must distinguish justice from revelation, show how divine love addresses lost relational opportunity, and establish that his permissive theology represents the traditional theism challenged by the motion.

moves.sectionTitle: Pluralism, experiential diversity, judgment, and the cumulative case
moves.currentDescription: Baker-Hytch concedes kaleidoscopic experiential diversity prevents religious experience alone from deciding among faiths, while treating some reported conversion asymmetries as potentially interesting but limited.
moves.lockedProposition: Religious experiences are unquestionably diverse and cannot by themselves decisively discriminate among religions, although some reported asymmetries may be evidentially interesting.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: um yeah um so religious experience and being diverse that seems unquestionably the case it is interesting that there are um actually a a significant number of accounts of people in majority Muslim countries who convert to Christianity because they claim to have visions and dreams of Jesus I'm not aware of a reverse phenomenon of Christians having visions and dreams of Muhammad so that is interesting um but yeah I mean at the end of the day I I think uh religious experience on its own is going to be if you want to stand back and try and take a sort of as objective a perspective on the situation as he can when you look at the kaleidoscopic diversity of religious uh religious experience in the world that that's going to doesn't seem like it's going to be a decisive way to try and um figure out which if any religion is more true than others Julian you got
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baker-Hytch candidly concedes that kaleidoscopic religious experience cannot independently discriminate among religions, thereby answering Baggini with careful calibration while preserving only a limited possible role for reported asymmetries. Principal limitation: The Muslim-to-Christian vision comparison is unsupported, lacks denominator or reverse-case evidence, and sits uneasily beside the broader concession that experience alone is indecisive. Live burden: He must document any genuine asymmetry, explain how cultural expectations affect reports, and specify the modest evidential contribution experience makes when combined with historical and philosophical arguments.

moves.sectionTitle: Pluralism, experiential diversity, judgment, and the cumulative case
moves.currentDescription: Baker-Hytch argues that non-apologetic historical Jesus scholarship, religious experience, and a stronger philosophical case for theism jointly make Christianity rationally entertainable, without providing proof.
moves.lockedProposition: Historical evidence concerning Jesus is not proof and did not persuade alone, but together with religious experience and a stronger philosophical case for theism it can make Christian belief rationally entertainable.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Baker-Hytch finally supplies the promised cumulative architecture, combining non-apologetic historical claims about Jesus with philosophical theism and limited experience while explicitly refusing to present the conjunction as proof. Principal limitation: Several contested historical propositions are summarized without detailed support, their dependence is not analyzed, and saying the package is rationally entertainable does not establish that it outweighs hiddenness. Live burden: He must compare likelihoods under Christian and rival hypotheses, prevent philosophical theism from circularly licensing miracle claims, and state how much each evidential strand contributes after cultural mediation.
